result.dimension: query.add({b: c}) semantics and its return value

rules.rule: add() APPENDS, never replaces. Even if the key already exists (once or many times, with or without a value), a new pair is appended and all pre-existing pairs are kept in their original order. There is no de-duplication, not even when the added key AND value are byte-identical to an existing pair.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?K=1' --b K --c 2 -> [http | h | /p | K=1&K=2 | http://h/p?K=1&K=2]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=1&x=2&x=3' --b x --c 4 -> [http | h | /p | x=1&x=2&x=3&x=4 | http://h/p?x=1&x=2&x=3&x=4]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?K=1' --b K --c 1 -> [http | h | /p | K=1&K=1 | http://h/p?K=1&K=1]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&a' --b a --c z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&a&a=z | http://h/p?a=1&a&a=z]

rules.rule: The new pair is always appended at the very END of the pair list (after every existing pair, including empty/valueless ones). Existing pair order is never reordered or sorted.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?z=9' --b a --c 1 -> [http | h | /p | z=9&a=1 | http://h/p?z=9&a=1] (not sorted). argv: --a 'http://h/p?b=2&a=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | b=2&a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?b=2&a=1&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&&Z=Z]

rules.rule: add() returns the SAME query object it mutated (self), so line4 == str(f.query) after mutation, and line4 is always exactly the substring of line5 between the '?' and the '#' (or end of string). Implement line4 and line5's query component from one shared serialization.
rules.evidence: Holds in every one of ~60 probes. e.g. argv: --a 'https://u:pw@h:8080/p?a=1#fr' --b Z --c Z -> [https | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | https://u:pw@h:8080/p?a=1&Z=Z#fr]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#f?q=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#f?q=2]

rules.rule: The ADDED pair is ALWAYS serialized as `encKey` + '=' + `encValue`. The '=' is always emitted, even when the value is the empty string. So: empty value -> 'K=' (never bare 'K'); empty key -> '=V'; both empty -> '='.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b K --c '' -> [http | h | /p | a=1&K= | http://h/p?a=1&K=]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b '' --c V -> [http | h | /p | a=1&=V | http://h/p?a=1&=V]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b '' --c '' -> [http | h | /p | a=1&= | http://h/p?a=1&=]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b '' --c '' -> [http | h | /p | = | http://h/p?=]

rules.rule: When the original URL has NO query at all, or an empty query ('?'), line4 is just the encoded pair with NO leading '&', and line5 becomes url + '?' + pair. '?' with nothing after it means ZERO pairs (not one empty pair).
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c V -> [http | h | /p | K=V | http://h/p?K=V]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?' --b K --c V -> [http | h | /p | K=V | http://h/p?K=V]. argv: --a 'http://h' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | (empty) | Z=Z | http://h?Z=Z]. argv: --a '?' --b Z --c Z -> [None | None | (empty) | Z=Z | ?Z=Z]

rules.rule: Pairs are joined with '&' only. Serialization is: for each pair, (key===None-valued ? encKey : encKey + '=' + encValue), joined by '&'.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&b&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&b&Z=Z] (valueless 'b' stays bare). argv: --a 'http://h/p?b&a=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | b&a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?b&a=1&Z=Z]

rules.rule: ENCODER (used identically for the added key, the added value, and every re-serialized original key/value): UTF-8 encode the string; for each byte, output the literal char if it is A-Z a-z 0-9 or one of '-' '.' '_' '~'; output '+' for space (0x20); otherwise output '%' + two UPPERCASE hex digits. This is Python quote_plus with safe=''. Note '!' '*' '(' ')' "'" are NOT safe (unlike JS encodeURIComponent).
rules.evidence: Full ASCII sweep on the value (--a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'X<ch>X', line4 shown): !->X%21X "->X%22X #->X%23X $->X%24X %->X%25X &->X%26X '->X%27X (->X%28X )->X%29X *->X%2AX +->X%2BX ,->X%2CX -->X-X .->X.X /->X%2FX :->X%3AX ;->X%3BX <->X%3CX =->X%3DX >->X%3EX ?->X%3FX @->X%40X [->X%5BX \->X%5CX ]->X%5DX ^->X%5EX _->X_X `->X%60X {->X%7BX |->X%7CX }->X%7DX ~->X~X space->X+X. Same for keys: --a 'http://h/p' --b 'K*K' --c V -> line4 'K%2AK=V'; --b 'K~K' -> 'K~K=V'; --b 'K K' -> 'K+K=V'; --b 'K+K' -> 'K%2BK=V'. Full transcript example: argv --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c ':@$,;' -> [http | h | /p | K=%3A%40%24%2C%3B | http://h/p?K=%3A%40%24%2C%3B]

rules.rule: Non-ASCII in key or value is UTF-8 encoded then percent-encoded byte-by-byte (uppercase hex). Control chars likewise (\n -> %0A, \t -> %09).
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'é' -> [http | h | /p | K=%C3%A9 | http://h/p?K=%C3%A9]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c '日本' -> [http | h | /p | K=%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC | http://h/p?K=%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b 'é' --c V -> [http | h | /p | %C3%A9=V | http://h/p?%C3%A9=V]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'ü ö' -> [http | h | /p | K=%C3%BC+%C3%B6 | http://h/p?K=%C3%BC+%C3%B6]

rules.rule: The key/value strings are treated as LITERAL text, not pre-encoded. A '%' the caller passes is escaped to '%25' (double-encoding), and '=' / '&' / '#' / '?' inside the key or value are escaped so they can never break out of their pair.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c '%2F' -> [http | h | /p | K=%252F | http://h/p?K=%252F]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c '%41' -> [http | h | /p | K=%2541 | http://h/p?K=%2541]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b Z --c '%3F' -> [http | h | /p | a=1&Z=%253F | http://h/p?a=1&Z=%253F]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'a&b=c' -> [http | h | /p | K=a%26b%3Dc | http://h/p?K=a%26b%3Dc]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b '&Z=1&' --c V -> [http | h | /p | a=1&%26Z%3D1%26=V | http://h/p?a=1&%26Z%3D1%26=V]

rules.rule: ORIGINAL query pairs ARE re-encoded: each original key/value is percent-DECODED (with '+' -> space) and then re-encoded with the same encoder as rule 7. Consequences: '%20' -> '+', a raw space -> '+', a literal '+' stays '+', '%2B' stays '%2B', '%7E' -> '~', '%41' -> 'A', lowercase hex is uppercased ('%2f' -> '%2F'), '%2F'/'%3A'/'%26'/'%3D'/'%23' stay percent-encoded.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a%2Bb' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a%2Bb&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a%2Bb&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a+b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a+b&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a+b&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a+b&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a+b&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a%20b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a+b&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a+b&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%7E%2F%3A' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=~%2F%3A&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=~%2F%3A&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%41%42%30' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=AB0&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=AB0&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?%2f' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | %2F&Z=Z | http://h/p?%2F&Z=Z]

rules.rule: Malformed percent escapes in the original query ('%' not followed by two hex digits) are decoded as a LITERAL '%' character and therefore re-encoded to '%25'.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=%25&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=%25&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%zz' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=%25zz&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=%25zz&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=%252&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=%252&Z=Z]

rules.rule: Original query parsing: split ONLY on '&' (';' is NOT a separator). Each segment is split at its FIRST '=' -> (key, value); any further '=' belong to the value and get re-encoded as '%3D'. A segment containing no '=' has value None and re-serializes as the bare encoded key (no trailing '='). A segment that is exactly '' yields an empty key with value None and re-serializes as ''.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1;b=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1%3Bb%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3Bb%3D2&Z=Z] (one pair, ';' not a separator). argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3D2&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1?b=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1%3Fb%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3Fb%3D2&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x&Z=Z | http://h/p?x&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=&Z=Z]

rules.rule: Empty segments from '&&', a leading '&' or a trailing '&' are preserved as empty pairs, so the '&' runs survive the round-trip and the added pair still goes after them.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&&b=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&&b=2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&&b=2&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?&' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | &&Z=Z | http://h/p?&&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?&a=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | &a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?&a=1&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&&Z=Z]

rules.rule: In line5 the added pair lands inside the QUERY component: after the path, after all existing pairs, and BEFORE the '#fragment'. If the URL previously had no query, a '?' is inserted before the fragment. Text that looks like a query but sits inside the fragment ('#f?q=1') is left in the fragment and is NOT merged.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#frag' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#frag]. argv: --a 'http://h/p#f?q=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | Z=Z | http://h/p?Z=Z#f?q=1]. argv: --a '#f' --b Z --c Z -> [None | None | (empty) | Z=Z | ?Z=Z#f]

rules.rule: add() itself never raises for any string key/value (including '', '=', '&', '#', '%', newlines, non-ASCII). Every nonzero-exit observed came from URL parsing of --a before add() ran (e.g. 'ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL', "ValueError: Invalid port '99999'."), producing a traceback on stderr and rc=1 with zero of the 5 lines printed.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://[bad?a=1' --b Z --c Z -> traceback ending 'ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL', rc=1, no output lines. argv: --a 'http://h:99999/p?a=1' --b Z --c Z -> traceback ending "ValueError: Invalid port '99999'.", rc=1. Contrast: argv --a 'http://h/p' --b '&' --c '&' -> [http | h | /p | %26=%26 | http://h/p?%26=%26] rc=0; argv --a 'http://h/p' --b '=' --c '=' -> [http | h | /p | %3D=%3D | http://h/p?%3D=%3D] rc=0

uncertainties: I could not pass a literal NUL byte through argv, so the encoding of \x00 in the ADDED key/value is untested (an original '%00' in the URL round-trips as '%00', so '%00' is the likely output).

Whether the internal representation distinguishes 'value is None' vs 'value is empty string' is inferred only from serialization: original segments without '=' print bare (e.g. 'x'), original segments with '=' print 'x='. The added pair always has a string value, so it always prints 'k=v'. I could not construct an added pair with a None value from the CLI (argparse type=str always yields a string).

Bytes 0x80-0xFF that are not valid UTF-8 cannot be passed via argv reliably, so behavior of the original query containing invalid-UTF-8 percent escapes (e.g. '?x=%FF') was not probed. '%C3%A9' round-trips unchanged, which suggests decode-to-text then re-encode, but a lone '%FF' may behave differently (surrogateescape) — untested.
Very long keys/values (>8KB) were not probed for truncation; no reason to expect any.

Whether a trailing '#' with an empty fragment is dropped from line5 was observed once ('http://h/p?a=1#' -> line5 'http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z', no '#'), but that belongs to the fragment dimension and was only tested once here.

rules.rule: Fragment placement in line5 (f.url) is ALWAYS scheme://netloc + path + '?' + query + '#' + fragment. The fragment is emitted LAST, after the query, and the added b=c pair NEVER lands in the fragment (it always goes to the main query, line 4).
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?q=1#f?g=2' --b Z --c Z  ->  'http'/'h'/'/p'/'q=1&Z=Z'/'http://h/p?q=1&Z=Z#f?g=2'   AND   argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=1&y=2#fp?fq=3&fr=4' --b n --c v -> 'http'/'h'/'/p'/'x=1&y=2&n=v'/'http://h/p?x=1&y=2&n=v#fp?fq=3&fr=4' (fragment query fq/fr untouched by add)

rules.rule: An EMPTY fragment does not survive: a trailing '#' with nothing after it is dropped from f.url entirely (no trailing '#'). Same for '#' at end of a host-only URL and for the whole input being '#'.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p#' --b Z --c Z -> 'http'/'h'/'/p'/'Z=Z'/'http://h/p?Z=Z' ; argv: --a 'http://h#' -> 'http'/'h'/''/'Z=Z'/'http://h?Z=Z' ; argv: --a 'http://h/p?q=1#' -> 'http'/'h'/'/p'/'q=1&Z=Z'/'http://h/p?q=1&Z=Z' ; argv: --a '#' -> 'None'/'None'/''/'Z=Z'/'?Z=Z'

rules.rule: PARSE MODEL. Let F = everything after the FIRST '#' in the URL (the '#' char and all later '#' belong to F only if they came after the first one -- see the %23 rule). Split F once at its first '?' into head and rest. (a) If F contains no '?', then: if F contains '=', fragment.query = F and fragment.path = ''; else fragment.path = F and fragment.query = ''. (b) If F contains '?' AND rest (everything after the first '?') contains '=', then fragment.path = head and fragment.query = rest. (c) If F contains '?' but rest contains NO '=', then the WHOLE F becomes fragment.path (the '?' chars stay literally in the path) and fragment.query = ''.

REASSEMBLY / SEPARATOR. str(fragment) = fragPathStr + ('?' if BOTH fragPathStr and fragQueryStr are non-empty else '') + fragQueryStr. Consequence: if the fragment path is empty, the leading '?' is DROPPED ('#?b=1' renders as '#b=1'). There is no parse that yields non-empty path + empty query with a real separator (case (c) folds the '?' into the path), so 'a?' is a path, not path+separator.
Only the FIRST '#' delimits the fragment. Every subsequent '#' is part of the fragment and is percent-encoded to '%23' in f.url.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p##x' --b Z --c Z -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#%23x  ;  argv: --a 'http://h/p#f#g' -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#f%23g  ; and an input '%23' round-trips: '#%23' -> http://h/p?Z=Z#%23

rules.rule: FRAGMENT PATH ENCODING. The fragment path is percent-DECODED on parse then RE-ENCODED. Left literal (unencoded): A-Za-z0-9 and - . _ ~ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; = : @ / ?  . Percent-encoded (uppercase hex): space->%20, '"'->%22, '#'->%23, '%'->%25, '<'->%3C, '>'->%3E, '['->%5B, '\'->%5C, ']'->%5D, '^'->%5E, '`'->%60, '{'->%7B, '|'->%7C, '}'->%7D, and every non-ASCII char as UTF-8 bytes percent-encoded. '+' is NOT treated as a space here (stays a literal '+').

FRAGMENT PATH PERCENT NORMALIZATION. Valid escapes are decoded then re-encoded per the safe set: '%41'->'A', '%3F'->'?', '%26'->'&', '%3D'->'=' (all emitted raw). '%2f' is normalized to uppercase '%2F' and stays encoded (encoded slash is preserved so it does not become a segment separator). '%25' stays '%25'. Malformed escapes ('%zz', '%2', bare '%') are treated as a literal '%' and re-encoded to '%25' with the rest kept literal.

FRAGMENT QUERY ENCODING (much stricter than the path). The query part is split on '&' into pairs, each split on the FIRST '=' into key/value; each is percent-decoded (with '+' decoded to a space) then re-encoded form-style: only A-Za-z0-9 and - . _ ~ are literal, space becomes '+', and every other byte becomes %XX (uppercase hex, UTF-8 for non-ASCII). '&' and '=' are re-emitted only as separators. A pair with no '=' in the source is re-emitted as a bare key with no '='.
rules.evidence: '#pp?k=a/b'->#pp?k=a%2Fb ; '#pp?k=a:b'->#pp?k=a%3Ab ; '#pp?k=a@b'->#pp?k=a%40b ; '#pp?k=a!b'->#pp?k=a%21b ; '#pp?k=a$b'->#pp?k=a%24b ; "#pp?k=a'b"->#pp?k=a%27b ; '#pp?k=a(b)'->#pp?k=a%28b%29 ; '#pp?k=a*b'->#pp?k=a%2Ab ; '#pp?k=a,b'->#pp?k=a%2Cb ; '#pp?k=a;b'->#pp?k=a%3Bb ; '#pp?k=a~b'->#pp?k=a~b ; '#p?k=a=b'->#p?k=a%3Db ; '#a?k=v w'->#a?k=v+w ; '#a?k=v%20w'->#a?k=v+w ; '#a?k=v+w'->#a?k=v+w ; '#a?k=hé'->#a?k=h%C3%A9 ; '#a?k=🎉'->#a?k=%F0%9F%8E%89 ; '#a?k=%41'->#a?k=A ; '#a?k=%zz'->#a?k=%25zz ; '#a?k'->#a?k ; '#a?k=v&k2'->#a?k=v&k2 . Full 5 lines for '#pp?k=a/b': http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#pp?k=a%2Fb

rules.rule: A '?' inside the fragment IS preserved as a literal '?' in f.url whenever it is the path/query separator (case b) or part of the fragment path (case c). It is only percent-encoded (%3F) when it ends up INSIDE a fragment-query key or value.

The fragment is preserved for URLs with no scheme/host and for non-hierarchical schemes; f.url still emits '?<query>#<fragment>' in that order. Fragment text case is NOT normalized (unlike scheme/host which are lowercased).
rules.evidence: '#f' -> None / None / '' / Z=Z / ?Z=Z#f ; '/p#f' -> None / None / /p / Z=Z / /p?Z=Z#f ; 'p#f' -> None / None / p / Z=Z / p?Z=Z#f ; '//h/p#f' -> None / h / /p / Z=Z / //h/p?Z=Z#f ; 'mailto:a@b.com#f' -> mailto / None / a@b.com / Z=Z / mailto:a@b.com?Z=Z#f ; 'HTTP://H/P#Frag' -> http / H... actually host prints 'h' -> http / h / /P / Z=Z / http://h/P?Z=Z#Frag (fragment 'Frag' keeps case)

rules.rule: TAB (0x09), LF (0x0A) and CR (0x0D) are stripped from the ENTIRE input URL before any parsing (Python urlsplit behavior), so they never appear in the fragment and can even change how the fragment splits into path/query.
rules.evidence: argv --a $'http://h/p#a\nb' -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#ab ; argv --a $'http://h/p#a\tb' -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#ab ; argv --a $'http://h/p#a\rb' -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#ab ; argv --a $'http://h/p#a?b\n=1' -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#a?b=1 (the stripped newline turns it into a path+query fragment)

rules.rule: A fragment consisting only of characters that encode to non-empty output still survives (it is not treated as empty); only a literally-empty fragment is dropped. E.g. '# ' keeps '#%20'.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p# ' --b Z --c Z -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z#%20 ; contrast argv: --a 'http://h/p#' -> http / h / /p / Z=Z / http://h/p?Z=Z

rules.rule: The fragment path is NOT normalized: no leading '/' is added, '//', '..', './' and trailing '/' are all left as-is.
No fragment input observed causes a crash; rc is 0 and 5 lines are always printed, including for malformed percent escapes, lone '#', empty --a, unicode, and control characters.
rules.evidence: rc=0 on all ~60 probes including --a '' , --a '#' , --a 'http://h/p#%' , --a 'http://h/p#a%2' , --a 'http://h/p#🎉' . e.g. --a '' --b Z --c Z -> None / None / '' / Z=Z / ?Z=Z with rc=0

uncertainties: I did not find a way, purely by parsing a URL string, to produce a fragment with a NON-empty path and an EMPTY query where a '?' separator is still emitted -- because whenever the text after the first '?' has no '=', furl folds the whole fragment into the path. So the rule 'emit ? only when both sides non-empty' and the rule 'furl keeps a separator flag set at parse time' are observationally indistinguishable here. Both implementations reproduce every probe I ran.

Whether the case-(b) trigger is exactly "'=' appears anywhere after the first '?'" vs "'=' appears in the segment between the 1st and 2nd '?' OR later" is settled for the cases I probed ('#a?b?c=1' -> path+query proves it looks at the whole remainder, not just the segment between the first two '?'), but I did not probe pathological inputs with 4+ '?' characters.

result.dimension: PATH — encoding, decoding, and reassembly (furl.path on line3 and inside furl.url on line5)

rules.rule: CORE MODEL (2-step, per segment). After the URL is split, the raw path string is split on literal '/' into segments. Each segment is then (1) FULLY percent-DECODED (UTF-8, errors='replace'), then (2) RE-ENCODED with a fixed safe set. Segments are rejoined with '/'. Output is therefore a canonical re-encoding, never the raw input bytes. Pseudo-JS: path.split('/').map(seg => encode(decode(seg))).join('/')
rules.evidence:
a='http://h/a%2fb' -> lines: http | h | /a%2Fb | Z=Z | http://h/a%2Fb?Z=Z   (lowercase hex upcased => decode+re-encode, not passthrough)
a='http://h/%41%42%43' -> http | h | /ABC | Z=Z | http://h/ABC?Z=Z   (decode happened)
a='http://h/a%252Fb' -> http | h | /a%252Fb | Z=Z | http://h/a%252Fb?Z=Z   (decode once to '%2F' then re-encode '%'->%25)

rules.rule: SAFE SET (left literal in an output path segment) = ALPHA / DIGIT / '-' '.' '_' '~' '!' '$' '&' "'" '(' ')' '*' '+' ',' ';' '=' ':' '@'. This is exactly RFC3986 pchar (unreserved + sub-delims + ':' + '@'). Every other character is percent-encoded as the UPPERCASE-hex UTF-8 bytes.
rules.evidence:
Full ASCII 0x20-0x7E scan with a='http://h/x<CH>y'. Literal: ! $ & ' ( ) * + , - . 0-9 : ; = @ A-Z _ a-z ~ . Examples:
a='http://h/x!y' -> http | h | /x!y | Z=Z | http://h/x!y?Z=Z
a='http://h/x~y' -> http | h | /x~y | Z=Z | http://h/x~y?Z=Z
a='http://h/x%21y' -> http | h | /x!y | Z=Z | http://h/x!y?Z=Z   (decoded '!' also stays literal)

rules.rule: ENCODED SET (ASCII chars that ARE percent-encoded inside a path segment), with exact output bytes: SPACE->%20, '"'->%22, '#'->%23, '%'->%25, '/'->%2F, '<'->%3C, '>'->%3E, '?'->%3F, '['->%5B, '\\'->%5C, ']'->%5D, '^'->%5E, '`'->%60, '{'->%7B, '|'->%7C, '}'->%7D, DEL(0x7F)->%7F, and all C0 controls 0x01-0x1F (except 0x09/0x0A/0x0D which are deleted earlier) -> %01..%1F. Hex digits are always UPPERCASE.
rules.evidence:
a='http://h/x[y' -> http | h | /x%5By | Z=Z | http://h/x%5By?Z=Z
a='http://h/x^y' -> http | h | /x%5Ey | Z=Z | http://h/x%5Ey?Z=Z

rules.rule: HEX CASE IS NORMALIZED TO UPPERCASE. Lowercase input escapes %2f, %c3%a9, %ef%bf%bd, %2e all come back uppercase (or decoded to a literal).
rules.evidence:

rules.rule: '/' NEVER APPEARS DECODED. %2F / %2f decode to '/', but because splitting into segments happened BEFORE decoding, the decoded '/' lives inside a segment and is re-encoded to %2F. So %2F round-trips to %2F, and a raw '/' stays a literal separator.

rules.rule: '+' IS NOT SPACE IN THE PATH. A raw '+' stays '+'; %2B decodes to '+' and stays '+'; a raw space becomes %20. (Contrast with the query on line4, where a space becomes '+'.)

result.dimension: QUERY PARSING (splitting the incoming query string into pairs, and re-serializing it)

rules.rule: Query extraction: the fragment is cut off first at the FIRST '#', then the query is everything after the FIRST '?' in the remainder. A '?' that appears after a '#' belongs to the fragment and is never parsed as a query. A second '?' inside the query is an ordinary literal query character (it percent-encodes to %3F).

argv: --a 'http://h/p#frag?x=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | Z=Z | http://h/p?Z=Z#frag?x=1   (query is EMPTY; the '?x=1' stayed in the fragment)
argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#f?x=2' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#f?x=2
argv: --a 'http://h/p??a=1' --b Z --c Z  ->  http | h | /p | %3Fa=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?%3Fa=1&Z=Z   (query string is '?a=1', key='?a')

rules.rule: Pre-processing: every ASCII TAB (0x09), LF (0x0A) and CR (0x0D) byte is REMOVED from the URL string before parsing (they vanish entirely, they are not encoded). No other control character is removed — 0x01, 0x0B (VT) and 0x0C (FF) survive and are percent-encoded. A raw space also survives (and becomes '+').

rules.rule: The query encoder is exactly Python urllib.parse.quote_plus(s, safe=''): the ONLY characters emitted literally are A-Z, a-z, 0-9, '-', '.', '_', '~'. ASCII space (0x20) is emitted as '+'. This safe set was verified exhaustively over ASCII 0x20-0x7E in both key and value position, plus controls 0x01-0x1F and 0x7F.

rules.rule: SCHEME DETECTION runs on the RAW --a string, before any whitespace or control-character processing. Algorithm: (1) if raw.startsWith(':') -> scheme = '' (empty string, prints as blank line). (2) else let prefix = raw truncated at the first occurrence of any of '#', '?', '/'; let i = prefix.indexOf(':'); if i <= 0 -> scheme = null. (3) else let cand = raw.slice(0, i); if cand[0] is NOT an ASCII letter [A-Za-z] -> scheme = null; otherwise scheme = cand.toLowerCase(). uncertainties: The internal decomposition into 'get_scheme on the raw string' + 'modified = http: + rest' + 'urlsplit' is inferred, not read. It reproduces all ~95 probes I ran, but it is a behavioral model. In particular I could not distinguish 'netloc presence = rest.startsWith("//") on the raw rest' from 'netloc presence = the substituted string has // immediately after the scheme colon, tested before tab/NL removal' — both give identical predictions on every probe I could construct. Either is safe to implement.

The scheme first-character test is confirmed as ASCII-letter-only ([A-Za-z]) by 8 rejections and ~15 acceptances, but I did not enumerate every non-letter byte. NUL (\x00) could not be tested because bash cannot pass it in argv.

str(f.path) for a scheme-less input never round-trips the discarded authority, so inputs like $'/\t/p' are irreversibly lossy. I verified two examples but did not enumerate the whole family of tab-broken slash sequences.

The exact percent-encoding set for the path was sampled (~30 characters), not exhaustively enumerated. Characters I did not test include the remaining C1/high-bit ranges beyond one UTF-8 example (é) and delimiters like '?' and '#' appearing pre-encoded as %3F/%23 in the middle of a segment (I only tested %2F and %3F).

The exact IDNA variant (idna vs uts46, and what happens on IDNA failure such as an over-long label or a leading hyphen) is unexplored and may be another crash source; it belongs to the host dimension rather than this one.

f.query was always non-empty in my probes because {b: c} is always added (minimum '='), so I could never observe whether f.url omits the '?' for an empty query. A JS port should still implement 'emit ? only if the query string is non-empty' for safety.

It may also contain 'file': -1 (unobservable, since a port must be 1..65535). If exactness matters, an implementer should treat the 45-entry map as complete but be aware of this residual risk.

The rule 'idna_decode runs only when the host startswith("xn--")' is inferred from the crash/no-crash asymmetry between 'xn--fsq.héllo' (crash) and 'héllo.xn--fsq' / 'h.xn--fsq' / 'a.xn--fsq.com' (no decode, no crash). It is strongly supported by 6 probes but I could not read the source to confirm the literal predicate; an alternative equivalent formulation would be 'apply .decode("idna") to the whole host only if its first label begins with xn--'.

Exactly which Unicode code points nameprep maps/removes/prohibits during idna_encode is stdlib stringprep behaviour; I sampled U+00A0, U+00AD, U+200B, U+3002, U+FF0E-class, ẞ, Ⅻ, İ, Σ. A JS port needs a full stringprep/nameprep (RFC 3491) implementation, NOT the modern UTS-46 IDNA used by browsers/whatwg-url — results differ (e.g. this program maps ß -> 'ss' and Ⅻ -> 'xii').

I did not test whether nameprep-prohibited characters (stringprep table C.*) in a non-ASCII host raise during idna_encode — all my non-ASCII probes succeeded. Presumably they raise UnicodeError: Invalid character.

Ports were only tested as the segment after the last ':' of the hostport; behaviour with multiple ':' in a non-bracketed host is covered by the 'Invalid port' path (e.g. 'http://h:h/p' -> Invalid port 'h') but I did not enumerate every multi-colon shape.

Line 5's rendering of a None host as 'http:///p' (an empty authority) is an interaction with the path/URL-assembly dimension; I confirmed the observable outputs but did not fully model when '//' is emitted for schemes with a None host and a relative path.

rules.rule: FRAGMENT SERIALIZATION (needed to reproduce the tail exactly): split the raw fragment at its FIRST '?'. If there is no '?', or the part after the first '?' contains no '=', the ENTIRE raw fragment is the fragment-path (percent-encoded path-style: space -> %20, % -> %25). Otherwise it is (path, query): if path is empty the '?' separator is SUPPRESSED and only the query is emitted; else path + '?' + query (query encoded form-style: space -> '+').

uncertainties: Host-non-empty + relative-path is unreachable through furl's parser (a '//' authority always leaves the path empty or '/'-rooted), so urlunsplit's "insert a leading '/' when the path is relative" branch could only be exercised via the empty-netloc/USES_NETLOC route ('http:foo' -> 'http:///foo'). A JS port should still implement the insertion for the truthy-netloc branch to match urlunsplit, but I could not confirm it directly.

I could not distinguish netloc==None from netloc=='' for USES_NETLOC schemes with host None (e.g. 'http:' vs 'http://' both print 'http://?K=V'), because urlunsplit produces the same string either way. The model "netloc is null iff host is null" reproduces every observed case; the alternative "netloc is '' when host is null and scheme is not null" is indistinguishable on this program's outputs.

IDNA: I used Node's url.domainToASCII (UTS-46) to model Python's str.encode('idna'); they agree on every host I probed (ü.com, ÜBER.com, 日本.jp, a.ü.), but the two algorithms differ on exotic inputs (labels >63 bytes, empty labels, disallowed codepoints, already-punycoded 'xn--' labels). Python's codec raises UnicodeError on such labels, which would crash the program; I did not probe those.

The fragment serialization rule (split at first '?', treat the tail as a query only if it contains '='; suppress the '?' when the fragment path is empty) is inferred from 12 targeted probes and is marked 'likely'. It belongs to the fragment dimension; the reassembly rule itself only needs str(f.fragment) appended after '#'.

The USES_NETLOC and DEFAULT_PORTS tables were measured on this exact frozen build (Python 3.12 / furl bundled by PyInstaller). 'rtsps' is in USES_NETLOC here, which differs from older CPython releases, so a JS port should hard-code the measured lists rather than derive them from a newer/older urllib.
The ':' fix-up (scheme=='') and the '//' fix-up (netloc=='' and scheme is None) are mutually exclusive on all reachable inputs, so their relative ordering is unobservable.

Whitespace handling on --a is odd and unresolved: '  http://h/p  ' yields scheme None / host None / path '/p%20%20', so the leading spaces defeat scheme detection while the authority is still consumed somewhere. That is a parsing-dimension artifact; the reassembly template still reproduced line5 exactly for it.
